prompt: A colleague with a Windows laptop has to run the team's XCUITest suite before a release. What does she need?
hint: Which program runs the tests, and where does it exist?

choices.text: Appium installed on Windows, with its XCUITest driver
choices.why: The client may be on Windows; the server for iOS has to run on a Mac with Xcode.

choices.text: A Mac with Xcode, hers or rented
choices.why: Right. Xcode and its simulator exist only on macOS, and a rented Mac in a data centre counts.

choices.text: The iOS Simulator for Windows, from Apple's site
choices.why: There is none: the simulator is part of Xcode, which is published for the Mac only.

choices.text: WSL with Ubuntu, where Swift 6 runs
choices.why: Swift runs there, and Swift Testing with it; XCUITest needs Xcode and a simulator, which do not.

prompt: Which of these can a tester do on a Linux computer, with no Mac anywhere?
hint: The outer ring of the figure.

choices.text: Run Swift Testing tests of a Swift package
choices.why: Right: Swift 6 runs on Linux, and the logic needs no screen.

choices.text: Review an XCUITest file and the cases it covers
choices.why: Right: reading needs no Xcode.

choices.text: Run that XCUITest file on an iOS simulator
choices.why: The simulator is part of Xcode, on macOS.

choices.text: Install a debug build on an iPhone over USB
choices.why: Xcode signs and installs it, and Xcode needs a Mac.

prompt: Besides a Mac with Xcode, what does the section say running the app on your own iPhone needs?
hint: Three things, one of them in the phone's settings.

choices.text: A paid Apple Developer Program membership, before anything else
choices.why: That is for TestFlight and the App Store; your own device works with a free account, with limits.

choices.text: A jailbroken phone
choices.why: Nothing in the section asks for one; Apple's own route is signing.

choices.text: An Apple Account, a signed build and Developer Mode
choices.why: Right. Xcode signs the build for your phone, and the phone must be switched to Developer Mode.

choices.text: The iOS Simulator set to the same iOS version
choices.why: A simulator and a phone are separate targets; one does not need the other.

prompt: In a Swift Testing test, `#expect(show.price == "R$ 65,00")` is false. What happens next?
hint: One of the two macros stops; this is the other one.

choices.text: The whole suite stops
choices.why: Neither macro stops other tests.

choices.text: It is recorded, and the test carries on
choices.why: Right. #expect reports both sides of the == and continues; #require is the one that stops.

choices.text: The test is retried once, then reported as failed
choices.why: Nothing in Swift Testing retries a failed check on its own.

choices.text: The test stops at that line, like #require would
choices.why: That is #require's behaviour, not #expect's.

prompt: Why does the test write `let first = try #require(shows.first)` rather than `#expect(shows.first != nil)`?
hint: What would the next line check if there were no first show?

choices.text: Because #expect cannot compare optionals
choices.why: It can; the difference is what happens after a failure.

choices.text: To make the test run faster
choices.why: Speed is the same; the point is stopping when the rest would be meaningless.

choices.text: Because #require also retries until the list loads
choices.why: It waits for nothing; it unwraps or stops.

choices.text: It stops the test if there is no show
choices.why: Right. It unwraps the show or stops there: with no first show, every later check would be checking nothing.

prompt: Match each piece of Swift Testing to what it does.
hint: The notes of the example.

pairs.right: marks a function as a test
records a failure and lets the test go on
stops the test where it fails
runs one test once per value

right_distractors: waits for an element to appear

prompt: The parameterised price test has four pairs, and only (8005, "R$ 80,05") fails. What does the report show?
hint: How are the runs of one parameterised test reported?

choices.text: The 8005 case failed and the other three passed
choices.why: Right. Each argument is reported on its own, so the failure names its own input.

choices.text: One failed test, with no way to tell which pair broke it
choices.why: Telling the pairs apart is exactly what a parameterised test adds.

choices.text: Four failures, because the cases share one function
choices.why: They share the code, not the result.

choices.text: Nothing, since parameterised tests stop at the first failing pair
choices.why: The other pairs still run and report.

prompt: A developer proposes testing the offline banner of the iOS Tickets with Swift Testing, because it runs on the team's cheap Linux machines. What do you answer?
hint: Split what is decided from what is drawn.

choices.text: Agree: Swift Testing can launch the app and read the banner
choices.why: It cannot launch the app or read a screen at all.

choices.text: Refuse: offline behaviour can only be tested on a real iPhone
choices.why: A simulator can test the screen, and the logic needs no device at all.

choices.text: Test the decision to fall back there, and the banner itself in XCUITest
choices.why: Right. Whether to fall back on the saved list is logic; whether the banner shows is a screen.

choices.text: Write it in XCTest instead, since XCTest runs on Linux too
choices.why: XCTest's UI half needs the simulator, so the machine is still a Mac.

prompt: An Espresso test sets Shows.baseUrl directly. How does the XCUITest test point the iOS app at boxoffice?
hint: Where does the test's code run?

choices.text: It sets the app's variable the same way, from Swift
choices.why: It runs in another process, so the app's variables are out of its reach.

choices.text: It edits the app's settings file before building
choices.why: Then every build would carry the test's address; the test asks at launch instead.

choices.text: launchEnvironment, set before launch and read by the app as it starts
choices.why: Right, and the app's developers have to write the line that reads it.

choices.text: It cannot: an iOS app always asks the address it shipped with
choices.why: Launch arguments and environment variables exist for exactly this.

prompt: A test writes `row.waitForExistence(timeout: 15)` on a line of its own, and the row never appears. What happens?
hint: What does the method return?

choices.text: The test fails at that line after 15 seconds
choices.why: It returns false and fails nothing on its own; that is why the lesson wraps it.

choices.text: It answers false, and the next tap fails instead
choices.why: Right. Inside XCTAssertTrue, the failure would be the wait, where the cause is.

choices.text: It waits forever, since the timeout only applies on a device
choices.why: The timeout applies everywhere; 15 seconds is the most it waits.

choices.text: XCUITest restarts the app and tries again
choices.why: Nothing restarts the app unless the test calls launch again.

prompt: On iOS, the counterpart of Android's resource id, which XCUITest finds an element by, is the accessibility ___.
hint: The SwiftUI modifier is named after it.

prompt: `app.buttons["Refresh"]` finds the button today, although the button's identifier is `refresh`. Why is it still the wrong handle?
hint: What else does the bracket match against?

choices.text: It is slower, because XCUITest searches labels last
choices.why: The cost is not speed; it is what breaks the test.

choices.text: It finds the button only on the simulator
choices.why: It finds it on a phone too, as long as the word stays the same.

choices.text: Identifiers are case-insensitive, so it matches by luck
choices.why: It matches the label, Refresh, not the identifier.

choices.text: It matched the label, which follows the copy
choices.why: Right: it fails when the word changes or the phone is set to Portuguese, lesson 14's trap on another platform.

prompt: The iOS app asks http://localhost:8080 inside the simulator. Where does the request go?
hint: Compare with lesson 14's 10.0.2.2.

choices.text: To the simulator's own port, as localhost goes on Android's emulator
choices.why: The simulator is a Mac program sharing the Mac's network, so localhost is the Mac.

choices.text: To boxoffice on the Mac
choices.why: Right. No special address is needed on iOS, unlike 10.0.2.2.

choices.text: Nowhere, because iOS forbids localhost
choices.why: iOS forbids plain HTTP by default, not localhost, and an exception allows it.

choices.text: To the runner app, which answers for the app
choices.why: The runner taps and reads; it serves no requests.

prompt: Put in order the steps to run the UI tests from a terminal on a Mac and look at the result.
hint: A name has to exist before it is used.
items: list the simulators with xcrun simctl list devices available
pick one of their names for -destination
read the exit code, and open the .xcresult in Xcode if a test failed

prompt: Why does the section expect an iOS pipeline to hold fewer UI tests than the Android one, for the same app?
hint: What kind of machine does each UI test need?

choices.text: Because XCUITest cannot run more than a few tests per run
choices.why: There is no such limit; the cost is per minute of machine.

choices.text: A macOS minute costs several times a Linux one on hosted CI
choices.why: Right, so the logic moves to Swift Testing on Linux and the screens keep only the journeys.

choices.text: Because iOS apps have fewer screens
choices.why: Nothing about the platform makes an app smaller.

choices.text: Because Apple forbids UI tests in CI
choices.why: Hosted CI runs them on rented Macs; only the price differs.

prompt: Where can `swift test` in ios/TicketsCore run?
hint: What does the package need?

choices.text: Only in Xcode, from the Test navigator
choices.why: Xcode is one place; the package needs only Swift.

choices.text: Only on an iOS simulator
choices.why: The package has no app and no screen, so no simulator is involved.

choices.text: Anywhere Swift 6 runs
choices.why: Right: macOS, Linux or Windows, Mac or not.

choices.text: Only on a real iPhone connected over USB
choices.why: A phone is the last thing a logic test needs.

prompt: Match each tool to where its test code runs.
hint: The second row of the table.

pairs.right: in the Android app's own process
in a runner app beside the iOS app
on a computer, talking HTTP to a server
with the logic, and no screen at all

prompt: Why is an Appium test of the iOS app no faster than the same test written in XCUITest?
hint: Follow one tap from the test to the screen.

choices.text: Because Appium runs the app on an emulator instead of a simulator
choices.why: Appium uses the same simulator; the difference is the path of each step.

choices.text: Because JavaScript is slower than Swift
choices.why: The language of the test hardly matters; the hops between programs do.

choices.text: Because Appium waits for every animation and XCUITest does not
choices.why: It is the other way round: XCUITest waits for the app to settle, Appium waits only where told.

choices.text: Its driver is XCUITest underneath, plus HTTP and a server
choices.why: Right. WebDriverAgent is an XCUITest runner, so Appium adds steps rather than skipping any.

prompt: Which of the three tools can name the app's own classes and objects, not only what the screen shows?
hint: Which one shares the app's process?

choices.text: Espresso
choices.why: Right. Inside the process it can reach R.id, the Show objects and Shows.baseUrl.

choices.text: XCUITest
choices.why: It runs in a runner app of its own and sees only the screen.

choices.text: Appium
choices.why: It sees the screen through a driver, from another computer even.

choices.text: All three
choices.why: Only the one inside the app's process can.

prompt: A company has native Android and iOS apps and two testers. They want one suite of the main journeys on both. What should the testers ask of the developers first?
hint: What does one Appium suite assume about two apps?

choices.text: That both apps be rewritten in React Native
choices.why: A rewrite is not a testing request; Appium drives two native apps as they are.

choices.text: That both apps name the same elements the same way
choices.why: Right. One suite works only if the two names agree; a translation table is the costlier fallback.

choices.text: That the developers stop writing Espresso and XCUITest tests
choices.why: Those keep their place lower in the pyramid; the journeys are a smaller suite on top.

choices.text: A Mac for each tester, so that Android runs faster
choices.why: A Mac is needed for the iOS half, and it does nothing for Android's speed.

prompt: The XCUITest suite passes on a developer's Mac and fails in CI on every test, at the first waitForExistence for a row. boxoffice runs on the developer's Mac. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Whose localhost is the simulator's localhost?

choices.text: The CI Mac's simulator is too slow for 15 seconds
choices.why: Possible in theory, but every test failing at the same wait points to an empty list, not a slow one.

choices.text: The rows' identifiers differ between the two Macs
choices.why: Identifiers are in the app's code, the same build on both.

choices.text: Nothing serves boxoffice on the CI Mac
choices.why: Right. The simulator's localhost is the Mac it runs on, so the pipeline must start boxoffice there first (lesson 12).

choices.text: App Transport Security blocks plain HTTP only in CI
choices.why: The rule is in the app's settings and is the same wherever it runs.

prompt: An Appium suite written for Android finds the third row with `$$('id=example.tickets:id/title')[2]`. It is pointed at the iOS Tickets of this lesson. What happens?
hint: Compare the two apps' names for a row.

choices.text: It works, because Appium translates resource ids into accessibility identifiers
choices.why: Appium passes the name through; it has no table between the two apps.

choices.text: It finds no rows: the iOS app names them show-<id>
choices.why: Right, and the package prefix means nothing on iOS either. The names have to be agreed first.

choices.text: It opens the wrong show, since the order differs
choices.why: Both apps list the same three shows; the failure comes before any order matters.

choices.text: It needs only platformName changed to iOS
choices.why: The capabilities change the driver, not the names inside the app.
